title: Farkas Dual Rays Do Not Improve LLM-Based Optimization Model Repair

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The purpose of the contribution is to test whether Farkas dual ray multipliers improve constraint ranking for truncated IIS feedback in LLM repair of infeasible optimization models. No prior paper explicitly addresses this purpose. Papers such as [1], [2], [6], [11], and [14] discuss infeasibility diagnosis and resolution in optimization models, but none test the specific hypothesis about Farkas dual ray multipliers improving IIS constraint ranking for LLM-based repair. Papers like [3], [5], [9], and [12] focus on IIS characterization or identification but do not address the use of Farkas dual rays for ranking constraints in the context of LLM repair. Thus, the purpose is uncovered.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves extracting the Farkas dual ray \( y \) from HiGHS (with presolve disabled) for an infeasible LP, ranking IIS constraints by \( |y_i| \) descending, and providing the top-K constraints (with or without normalized weights) to the LLM for one-step repair. Papers such as [3], [5], [6], [9], [12], and [21] discuss Farkas dual rays or IIS-related methods, but none describe the specific mechanism of ranking IIS constraints by \( |y_i| \) descending and integrating this ranking into an LLM repair pipeline. While [3] generalizes Farkas' lemma to semidefinite systems and [21] discusses exact duals and certificates of infeasibility, neither paper applies these concepts to ranking IIS constraints for LLM-based repair. Thus, the mechanism is uncovered.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves a training-free feedback interface with three conditions (IIS-TopK baseline, DualRay-TopK, DualRay+Weights) on MAMO-Optimization, with IIS/dual ray computed on LP relaxations for MIPs. Papers such as [8], [13], and [16] discuss LLM-based optimization modeling and evaluation setups, but none use the specific evaluation design described here. While [8] introduces OptiHive for LLM-based optimization pipelines and [16] benchmarks LLMs on network optimization problems, neither paper employs the same feedback interface design or conditions. Thus, the evaluation is uncovered.

### Domain
The domain is LLM-based optimization modeling and solver-in-the-loop repair. Papers such as [8], [13], and [16] clearly operate in this domain. For example, [8] discusses enhancing LLM-based solvers, [13] addresses optimization modeling with LLMs, and [16] benchmarks LLMs on optimization problems. Although the specific sub-problem of infeasible optimization model repair is new, the general application area of LLM-based optimization modeling is covered. Thus, the domain is covered.

The mechanism involves controlled experiments holding model (Qwen2.5-7B), K=5, and greedy decoding fixed across three feedback conditions, with extended experiments varying K, samples, and model scale (32B, 72B). The evaluation design is therefore uncovered.

The domain is feedback-format ablation for infeasibility repair. Papers such as [1], [5], [13], [20], and [23] address infeasibility repair and irreducible infeasible subsystems, which fall within the same general application area. **PURPOSE: Show that simple regeneration beats solver-feedback repair on this benchmark.**

The purpose is to demonstrate empirically that simple resampling (Best-of-2) outperforms iterative solver-feedback repair. Paper [18] "Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?" directly investigates whether self-repair actually improves over simpler baselines, finding that "its efficacy thus remains poorly understood" and questioning repair's value. This is the same empirical relationship: regeneration/resampling vs. repair, with the finding that repair may not be superior. Paper [29] also revisits self-debugging and compares against baselines. Paper [18] is the closest match — it establishes the same relationship (simple regeneration competitive with or better than repair) in code generation.

**MECHANISM: Compare solver-feedback repair configurations against simple Best-of-2 inference scaling on the same 7B model.**

The mechanism is a controlled comparison of repair vs. Best-of-N sampling on the same model. Paper [18] uses exactly this design: comparing self-repair against simple resampling baselines on the same model. Paper [26] "On Sample-Efficient Code Generation" also compares sampling strategies against repair. The primitive — "run repair methods and Best-of-N sampling on the same model, compare pass rates" — is present in [18] and [26].

**EVALUATION: Best-of-2 achieves 65.12% Pass@1, outperforming all repair methods.**

The evaluation design uses Pass@1 as the metric and compares repair vs. sampling configurations. Paper [18] uses Pass@1 (or equivalent pass-rate metrics) to compare self-repair against resampling baselines. Paper [29] similarly uses pass-rate metrics comparing self-debugging against sampling baselines. The evaluation design (pass-rate metric, repair vs. sampling comparison) is covered by [18].

**DOMAIN: Inference-time scaling vs repair for optimization modeling.**

The domain is optimization modeling (mathematical programming / constraint solving). None of the prior papers address optimization modeling (LP/MIP formulation, etc.) as their application area. The prior papers cover code generation, math reasoning, LLM alignment, and general reasoning — not optimization modeling specifically. However, the broader area could be argued as "code/program generation with solver feedback." The closest is code generation with execution feedback ([18], [25], [29]), but optimization modeling (generating solver-ready formulations) is a distinct application area not covered by any prior paper.
